cards.front: Trace catecholamine synthesis from phenylalanine and name the rate-limiting enzyme.
cards.back: Phenylalanine is hydroxylated to tyrosine, tyrosine hydroxylase converts it to DOPA (the rate-limiting step), and DOPA decarboxylase gives dopamine. Dopamine enters the storage vesicle, where dopamine beta-hydroxylase converts it to noradrenaline. In adrenal medullary cells, phenylethanolamine N-methyltransferase (PNMT), induced by the high local cortisol level, methylates noradrenaline to adrenaline.

cards.front: Which drug blocks catecholamine synthesis, and where is it used?
cards.back: Metyrosine (alpha-methyl-p-tyrosine) inhibits tyrosine hydroxylase and depletes catecholamines. It is used to reduce catecholamine output in pheochromocytoma before surgery and in inoperable cases.

cards.front: How is noradrenaline stored in the nerve terminal, and how does reserpine act?
cards.back: It is held in vesicles, complexed with ATP (about 4:1) and bound to chromogranin. VMAT-2 pumps amines into the vesicle in exchange for H+. Reserpine blocks VMAT-2, so transmitter leaks into the cytoplasm, is destroyed by MAO, and the stores become depleted.

cards.front: Compare uptake-1 and uptake-2 for catecholamines.
cards.back: Uptake-1 is the Na+-coupled norepinephrine transporter (NET) in the neuronal membrane. It recaptures 75 to 90 percent of released noradrenaline, is blocked by cocaine and desipramine, and is the main way neuronal action ends. Uptake-2 is an extraneuronal transporter in other tissues. It is Na+-independent, prefers adrenaline, is not blocked by cocaine, and is quantitatively minor.

cards.front: Which enzymes metabolise catecholamines, and why does metabolism matter little for neuronally released noradrenaline?
cards.back: MAO acts first on the intraneuronal and leaked pool; COMT acts first on circulating amines in liver and other tissues. Aldehyde reductase, dehydrogenases and ADH take part in the intermediate steps. Urinary products are VMA, MOPEG, metanephrines and DOMA, mostly conjugated. Metabolism is slow compared with reuptake, so it contributes little to ending neuronal action.

cards.front: Using the Ahlquist classification, compare the potency order of adrenaline, noradrenaline and isoprenaline at alpha and beta receptors.
cards.back: Alpha: adrenaline greater than or equal to noradrenaline, both much greater than isoprenaline. Beta: isoprenaline greater than adrenaline, which is greater than or equal to noradrenaline. Ahlquist (1948) used these two distinct rank orders of agonist potency to divide adrenoceptors into alpha and beta; the split was later confirmed by selective antagonists.

cards.front: Compare alpha-1 and alpha-2 receptors: location, transducer, effector and selective drugs.
cards.back: Alpha-1 is postjunctional on effector organs. It acts through Gq, IP3/DAG and calcium, causing vasoconstriction, mydriasis and contraction of the bladder trigone and prostate. Phenylephrine is the selective agonist and prazosin the selective antagonist. Alpha-2 is mainly prejunctional, where it inhibits transmitter release, and is also found in the brain and platelets. It acts through Gi, lowering cAMP. Clonidine is the selective agonist and yohimbine the antagonist.

cards.front: Where are beta-1, beta-2 and beta-3 receptors found, and which selective drugs act on them?
cards.back: Beta-1: heart and juxtaglomerular cells; dobutamine is the relatively selective agonist, and metoprolol or atenolol the antagonists. Beta-2: bronchi, blood vessels, uterus, liver, skeletal muscle; salbutamol and terbutaline are agonists, ICI 118551 an antagonist. Beta-3: adipose tissue and bladder detrusor; mirabegron is the agonist used in overactive bladder.

cards.front: Dobutamine: receptor action, clinical dose and why it is useful as an inotrope.
cards.back: It is a dopamine derivative with no dopamine-receptor activity. Its main action is a relatively beta-1 selective agonism. At 2 to 8 mcg/kg/min IV it raises contractility and output with little change in peripheral resistance or BP, and less tachycardia than isoprenaline. It is less arrhythmogenic than adrenaline. Uses: pump failure after MI or cardiac surgery, short-term severe heart failure, and pharmacological stress testing.

cards.front: Describe ephedrine: mechanism, duration and why its use is now restricted.
cards.back: A mixed-acting sympathomimetic: it releases noradrenaline and also acts directly on alpha and beta receptors. It resists MAO, so it is orally active and lasts 4 to 6 hours, but it is about 100 times less potent than adrenaline, and tachyphylaxis develops on repeated doses. Its use is restricted because it lacks selectivity and its efficacy is low. Remaining uses: hypotension during spinal anaesthesia, mild chronic bronchial asthma, and occasionally postural hypotension.

cards.front: What is the drug of choice in anaphylactic shock, what is the dose, and why?
cards.back: Adrenaline, injected intramuscularly without delay: 0.5 mg (0.5 mL of 1 in 1000) in adults, 0.3 mL for children 6 to 12 years and 0.15 mL up to 6 years; repeat every 5 to 10 minutes if there is no or only transient improvement. It raises BP, counters bronchospasm and laryngeal oedema, acts fast, and also suppresses mediator release from mast cells. IV adrenaline is used only for immediately life-threatening shock, diluted and infused slowly with monitoring. H1 antihistamines and IV hydrocortisone are adjuncts only.

cards.front: What is the vasomotor reversal of Dale, and why does noradrenaline not show it?
cards.back: After alpha blockade, adrenaline's pressor effect turns into a fall in BP. Adrenaline at ordinary doses causes alpha-1 vasoconstriction and beta-2 vasodilatation. Blocking alpha leaves only the beta-2 vasodilatation. Noradrenaline has no beta-2 action, so its pressor effect persists after alpha blockade.

cards.front: Classify: catecholamine synthesis
cards.text: Catecholamines are made from {{phenylalanine}} via tyrosine and {{DOPA}} to dopamine; the rate-limiting enzyme is {{tyrosine hydroxylase}}, blocked by {{metyrosine}}.

cards.front: Classify: adrenergic receptor coupling and location
cards.text: Alpha-1 receptors couple to {{Gq}} and raise {{IP3/DAG}}; alpha-2 receptors couple to {{Gi}} and lower {{cAMP}}; beta-1 receptors are mainly in the {{heart}}; beta-2 receptors are mainly in {{bronchial}} smooth muscle.

cards.front: Classify: sympathomimetic drugs by mechanism
cards.text: Tyramine and amphetamine are {{indirect}} sympathomimetics; {{ephedrine}} and {{mephentermine}} are {{mixed-acting}}; {{phenylephrine}} is a selective {{alpha-1}} agonist.

cards.front: Classify: drugs acting on noradrenergic neurones
cards.text: {{Cocaine}} and {{desipramine}} block NET and potentiate noradrenaline; {{reserpine}} blocks VMAT-2 and depletes stores; {{selegiline}} inhibits MAO-B; {{entacapone}} inhibits COMT.

cards.front: Classify: uses of selective beta-2 agonists
cards.text: Selective beta-2 agonists are used in {{bronchial asthma}} and COPD, to delay {{preterm labour}} (ritodrine), and in {{familial hyperkalaemic periodic paralysis}}.

cards.front: Why do alpha-1 blockers cause postural hypotension?
cards.back: They block alpha-1 mediated constriction of arterioles and veins, so peripheral resistance and venous tone fall and blood pools in capacitance vessels. Venous return and cardiac output drop, and the postural reflex that normally compensates on standing is impaired, so BP falls on standing and dizziness or syncope can follow.

cards.front: Describe phenoxybenzamine: mechanism, duration and uses.
cards.back: A halogenated alkylamine that forms a reactive intermediate and covalently binds alpha receptors. The blockade is irreversible and non-equilibrium and lasts 3 to 4 days until new receptors are made. Its main effects are postural hypotension, nasal stuffiness, miosis and failure of ejaculation. It is used mainly in pheochromocytoma and occasionally in peripheral vascular disease. Oral dose 20 to 60 mg/day; i.m. and s.c. injection is painful and should be avoided.

cards.front: What is phentolamine used for, and what does its diagnostic test involve?
cards.back: It is a short-acting, nonselective alpha-1 and alpha-2 antagonist; alpha-2 block increases noradrenaline release, so reflex tachycardia is marked. Uses: hypertensive episodes in pheochromocytoma, clonidine withdrawal or cheese reaction, local infiltration for extravasation of noradrenaline or dopamine, and intracavernosal injection with papaverine. Book test: 5 mg IV over 1 minute; a fall above 35 mm Hg systolic or 25 mm Hg diastolic suggests pheochromocytoma, but false results occur. Katzung notes it is now rarely used, and diagnosis rests on raised plasma or urinary catecholamines and metanephrines.

cards.front: Prazosin: selectivity, first-dose effect and why it replaced phenoxybenzamine.
cards.back: It is a selective alpha-1 blocker (about 1000 times more selective for alpha-1 than alpha-2) that blocks all alpha-1 subtypes equally. Sparing prejunctional alpha-2 keeps reflex tachycardia mild. The first-dose effect (postural syncope) is reduced by starting with a low dose at bedtime, and tolerance to it develops. Being competitive and short acting (half-life 2 to 3 h, effect 6 to 8 h), it is easier to control than irreversible phenoxybenzamine. Uses: hypertension, BHP and Raynaud's phenomenon.

cards.front: Tamsulosin: receptor profile, advantages and key adverse effects in BHP.
cards.back: It is a uroselective alpha-1A/1D blocker. The 1A subtype dominates in the prostate and bladder base, so it relieves BHP symptoms with little change in BP or heart rate and little postural hypotension. It lacks the apoptosis-promoting effect seen with terazosin and doxazosin. Side effects: retrograde ejaculation and dizziness. Floppy iris syndrome is a concern during cataract surgery. It is given once daily as a modified-release capsule.

cards.front: Why do alpha-1 blockers relieve BHP faster than finasteride, and what do they not do?
cards.back: BHP obstruction has a static part (enlarged gland) and a dynamic part (alpha-1 mediated tone of the bladder neck and prostate). Alpha-1 blockers relax the dynamic part and give relief within about 2 weeks. Finasteride acts on the static part and takes around 6 months. Alpha-1 blockers do not reduce prostate size, and the benefit stops when the drug is stopped.

cards.front: Alfuzosin: duration, indication and key drug interaction.
cards.back: A short-acting prazosin congener (half-life about 3 to 5 hours), nonselective among alpha-1 subtypes. It is indicated only for symptomatic BHP and is not approved as an antihypertensive. It is metabolised by CYP3A4, so strong inhibitors such as erythromycin, ketoconazole and ritonavir should be avoided. Dose: 10 mg OD as extended release.

cards.front: Labetalol: receptor action, clinical niche and main side effect.
cards.back: It blocks alpha-1 and nonselectively blocks beta receptors, with beta blockade about 3 to 5 times stronger than alpha. Its fall in BP comes from alpha-1 block plus beta-2 vasodilatation. Heart rate is usually unchanged and limb blood flow increases. It is used in pheochromocytoma, clonidine withdrawal, pregnancy-induced hypertension and hypertensive emergencies (20 to 40 mg IV repeated). Its main side effect is postural hypotension.

cards.front: Propranolol: why does the antihypertensive effect appear only after some weeks?
cards.back: Acutely, propranolol lowers cardiac output, and total peripheral resistance rises, so BP changes little. With chronic use, resistance vessels adapt to the lower output, peripheral resistance falls and BP drops. Other contributions: less renin release (beta-1 mediated), less noradrenaline release, and central effects of lipophilic agents.

cards.front: Which beta-blockers have intrinsic sympathomimetic activity, and what advantages does it give?
cards.back: Pindolol, acebutolol and celiprolol. They partly activate beta receptors, so resting bradycardia and cardiac depression are minimal, exercise tachycardia is still blocked, rebound after withdrawal is less likely, and plasma lipids are less affected. Limitations: they are not useful for migraine prophylaxis (they dilate cerebral vessels) and are not suited to secondary prevention after MI.

cards.front: Esmolol: why is it so short acting, and where is it used?
cards.back: It is a cardioselective beta-1 blocker without partial agonist or membrane-stabilising action. Blood esterases hydrolyse it rapidly, so plasma half-life is under 10 minutes and the effect ends 15 to 20 minutes after stopping the infusion. It is given as a 0.5 mg/kg loading dose, then 0.05 to 0.2 mg/kg/min. Uses: supraventricular tachycardia, intraoperative arrhythmias, control of HR and BP during cardiac surgery and aortic dissection, and early MI.

cards.front: Why must membrane-stabilising beta-blockers be avoided in glaucoma eye drops, and what makes timolol the prototype?
cards.back: Membrane-stabilising agents anaesthetise the cornea and can damage it. Timolol is nonselective, lipophilic, and has no local anaesthetic or intrinsic sympathomimetic activity. It lowers intraocular pressure by 20 to 35 percent within an hour, for about 12 hours. Systemic absorption through the nasolacrimal duct can cause bronchospasm and bradycardia, so pressure on the inner canthus is advised after instillation.

cards.front: Classify: alpha-1 blocker subtype selectivity
cards.text: Prazosin blocks all alpha-1 subtypes {{equally}}; tamsulosin is selective for {{1A/1D}} subtypes; {{alfuzosin}} is nonselective among alpha-1 subtypes.

cards.front: Classify: beta-blockers by lipid solubility and elimination
cards.text: Lipophilic beta-blockers such as {{propranolol}} and {{metoprolol}} are cleared mainly by the {{liver}}; hydrophilic ones such as {{atenolol}} and {{sotalol}} are excreted largely {{unchanged in urine}}.

cards.front: Classify: antiglaucoma drugs by mechanism
cards.text: {{Latanoprost}} and {{travoprost}} are PGF2-alpha analogues that mainly increase {{uveoscleral}} outflow; {{timolol}}, a nonselective beta-blocker, mainly lowers aqueous {{secretion}}.

cards.front: Classify: carbonic anhydrase inhibitors and miotics in glaucoma
cards.text: {{Acetazolamide}} (oral) and {{dorzolamide}} (topical) inhibit {{carbonic anhydrase}} in the ciliary body and reduce aqueous formation; {{pilocarpine}} is a miotic that improves {{trabecular}} outflow.

cards.front: Classify: acute angle closure glaucoma measures
cards.text: Osmotic agent: {{mannitol}}; IV carbonic anhydrase inhibitor: {{acetazolamide}}; miotic: {{pilocarpine}} once pressure falls; topical beta-blocker: {{timolol}}; definitive treatment: {{laser iridotomy}}.
